title: Course final: memory in .NET
sub: From OS pages to pinning and Native AOT
cards/0/q: What is true about a process’s memory numbers? Select all.
cards/0/options/0: Virtual size includes reserved but uncommitted addresses
cards/0/options/1: Private bytes grow on commit, even if the pages were never touched
cards/0/options/2: The managed heap size includes memory from NativeMemory.Alloc
cards/0/options/3: Working set is the process’s pages currently in physical memory
cards/0/options/4: GC.GetTotalMemory shows the process’s private bytes
cards/0/explain: The numbers nest: virtual size ⊇ private bytes ⊇ what the GC heap occupies. The collector does not see native memory and does not count it in the heap size, and GC.GetTotalMemory counts only managed objects.
cards/1/q: A thread allocates an object and there is no room. Put what happens next in order
cards/1/items/0: The thread’s allocation chunk is used up — the slow path
cards/1/items/1: The gen 0 budget is exhausted — a collection is needed
cards/1/items/3: Marking: walk from the roots and through the card table
cards/1/items/5: Compaction: survivors slide, references are updated
cards/1/explain: A collection is triggered by an allocation, not a timer. The card table lets a young-generation collection find references into it from old objects without walking the whole heap. Pinned objects stay put during compaction.
cards/2/q: Where does the memory end up?
cards/2/pairs/4/1: The C library heap, outside the GC
cards/3/q: A Server GC service runs on a 32-core machine with a 1 GB memory limit. Load is light, yet the heap takes far more than the live data. What helps?
cards/3/options/0: DATAS (on by default for Server GC in .NET 9) or capping the heap count with GCHeapCount
cards/3/options/3: Calling GC.AddMemoryPressure with the heap size
cards/3/explain: Server GC keeps a heap and a gen 0 budget per core: 32 heaps is a lot of memory even under light load. DATAS adapts the number of heaps to the load, GCHeapCount caps it explicitly. Workstation GC is an option too.
cards/3/wrong/1: Full blocking collections every second add pauses, and the budgets for 32 heaps stay where they are.
cards/3/wrong/2: SustainedLowLatency suppresses blocking full collections — the heap only gets bigger.
cards/4/q: Windows get closed and forgotten, but the collector never collects them. Which line keeps them alive?
cards/4/explain: The Redraw delegate holds a reference to the window (Target), and a static event is a root that lives for the whole process. Until the window unsubscribes, it is reachable. The cure is unsubscribing on close or weak subscriptions.
cards/5/q: What does this method allocate on the heap on every call, in any .NET version?
cards/5/options/0: A closure object with a limit field, and a delegate
cards/5/options/1: Nothing: the lambda becomes a static method
cards/5/options/3: An array for a params argument
cards/5/explain: The lambda captures limit, so the compiler creates a closure class, an instance of it and a delegate to its method — on every call. A lambda with no captures would be cached by the compiler in a static field. Depending on the version, a boxed enumerator inside Count may come on top.
cards/5/wrong/2: A delegate without captures is indeed cached, but this one points to the closure object, and that is new on every call.
cards/6/q: A native library remembers a buffer’s address while the connection is open. There are a thousand buffers, needed for the whole run. What do you pick?
cards/6/options/0: A pool of arrays from GC.AllocateArray(..., pinned: true)
cards/6/options/1: A new byte[] per connection plus GCHandle.Alloc(..., Pinned)
cards/6/options/2: fixed in the method that hands the address to the library
cards/6/explain: Buffers in the POH never move and leave no holes in the young generations. A thousand fresh arrays with long pins is exactly the case that fragments the heap.
cards/6/wrong/2: A fixed pin ends with its block, while the library keeps writing to the address.
cards/6/wrong/3: stackalloc memory vanishes when the method returns — the library would write into someone else’s stack frame.
cards/7/options/0: TryStartNoGCRegion may run a full collection before the region starts
cards/7/options/1: The collector updates a ref T during compaction, but not a T* pointer
cards/7/options/2: Native AOT has no garbage collector
cards/7/options/4: Memory from NativeMemory.Alloc has to be freed by you
cards/7/explain: Native AOT uses the same collector as CoreCLR. AddMemoryPressure only hints to the collector that native memory stands behind objects — freeing it is still your job.
cards/8/q: n comes from outside. Put a small buffer on the stack and a large one on the heap
cards/8/explain: A thread’s stack is limited (usually 1 to 8 MB), and stackalloc sized by input can overflow it — which ends the process. So only a small buffer of known size goes on the stack; a large one goes on the heap or comes from ArrayPool.
